note: Patterns are heuristics, not bank-published formats: each is a case-insensitive regular expression searched in the raw transaction description, so plain text works as a substring; most patterns start at a word boundary (\b). Banks word fees differently and change wording, so expect misses and the odd false match; check that the line is a small debit before flagging it, and ignore lines that match exclude_patterns (refunds and reversals of a fee are credits). Kinds are checked in file order and the first match wins, so more specific kinds come first. Reversal tips describe what people can ask for; banks and card issuers decide case by case and nothing here guarantees a refund.

fees.label: ATM fee (out-of-network fee or operator surcharge)
fees.rule: Both your own bank and the ATM's owner can charge a fee for using another bank's ATM. Your bank must disclose its fee in writing when you open the account or when it adds a new fee; the ATM operator must disclose its fee at the machine.
fees.reversal_tip: Some banks and credit unions rebate ATM fees, so check the account's fee schedule; if a charge looks wrong or was never disclosed, ask the bank about a refund.
fees.notes: Lines like 'NON-WF ATM WITHDRAWAL' are usually the cash withdrawal itself, not the fee, so ATM patterns require FEE/CHARGE/SURCHARGE.

fees.label: Wire transfer fee
patterns: \bWIRE( TRANSFER| TRANS| XFER| TRF)?( OUT| IN| INCOMING| OUTGOING| DOMESTIC| DOM| INTL| INTERNATIONAL)? (FEE|CHARGE|CHG)
fees.rule: No federal law caps wire transfer fees; each bank sets its own, subject to any state law that applies.
fees.reversal_tip: Compare the charge with the bank's fee schedule; some account tiers waive incoming or outgoing wire fees, and a fee charged above the disclosed amount is worth disputing.

fees.label: Foreign transaction fee
fees.rule: A foreign transaction fee is any charge a card issuer adds for a purchase made outside the US, in a foreign currency, or with a foreign merchant (online too). It can combine a network charge and an issuer charge. Card issuers must disclose it in the card's rates and fees.
fees.reversal_tip: Fees on purchases from a merchant that looked domestic are worth questioning with the issuer; otherwise the usual fix is a card without foreign transaction fees for future travel.

fees.label: Returned payment fee (credit card or loan payment that bounced)
fees.rule: A credit card penalty fee can't exceed the dollar amount associated with the violation, and the issuer can't charge more than one penalty fee for a single event: e.g. a late fee and a returned-payment fee for the same bounced payment (Regulation Z, 12 CFR 1026.52(b)).
fees.reversal_tip: If a late fee and a returned-payment fee were both charged for the same bounced payment, ask the issuer to remove one; you can also ask for a one-time waiver.

fees.label: Late payment fee
fees.rule: Credit card late fees are limited by Regulation Z 12 CFR 1026.52(b): the fee must reflect the issuer's costs or fit a safe harbor, can't exceed the minimum payment that was due, and only one penalty fee may be charged per event. No dollar cap is given here: the CFPB's 2024 $8 late-fee rule was vacated by a federal court in April 2025 (eCFR still prints its text, while the CFPB's own regulation page shows the older safe-harbor text).
fees.reversal_tip: You can ask the issuer to waive a late fee, for example a first one paid soon after the due date; a late fee larger than the minimum payment that was due is not allowed.

fees.label: Overdraft fee
fees.rule: Banks may not charge an overdraft fee on ATM withdrawals or one-time debit card purchases unless the customer opted in to overdraft coverage (Regulation E, 12 CFR 1005.17). Checks and recurring payments can be charged without opt-in. Customers can withdraw from overdraft coverage at any time.
fees.reversal_tip: Ask the bank to refund the fee, especially a first one or one on a debit card or ATM transaction if you never opted in; if you never opted in and were charged for a debit/ATM overdraft, you can complain to the CFPB.

fees.label: Non-sufficient funds (NSF) / returned item fee
fees.rule: A bank can charge a fee when a check overdraws the account (a non-sufficient funds or NSF fee) as long as the practice was disclosed beforehand; the deposit account agreement lists the bank's fees.
fees.reversal_tip: Ask the bank to waive it, especially if several NSF fees were charged for the same payment being re-presented, or if a deposit was pending; check the account agreement for its rules.

fees.label: Monthly maintenance / service fee
fees.rule: An account advertised as 'free' or 'no cost' can't charge a monthly service fee, a minimum-balance fee, or per-transaction fees; it can still charge fees such as ATM, overdraft, bounced-check or stop-payment fees.
fees.reversal_tip: Check how the bank waives the fee (often a minimum balance or direct deposit); if the account was sold as free, or you met the waiver terms, ask for a refund. Moving to a no-fee account stops it for good.
